newsitem.title: USA: Medical dramas to grab spotlight at Emmy awards.
newsitem.headline: Medical dramas to grab spotlight at Emmy awards.

text.p: "E.R." and "Chicago Hope" are expected to be the big winners at the 48th Emmy Awards Sunday, showing that TV viewers have not yet lost their fascination with doctors and emergency room drama.

For the second straight year, hospital shows, along with upscale urban sitcoms like "Frasier" are up for multiple honors. And NBC, which airs both "E.R.", "Frasier," and a host of other hits is poised to walk away with most of the awards once again.

With so many repeat performances taking away from the suspense, even the networks themselves are sounding a little blase about the whole event. Most of the top nominated shows, after all, have already won the contest that counts the most, the one with audiences.

Regardless of who takes the most awards this year, several critics believe a more stunning achievement is the large number of nominations that went to cable stations that have only a fraction of the networks' viewers.

Home Box Office (HBO), for instance, is up for some 66 awards, putting it in third place in terms of overall nominations. NBC was nominated 88 times, CBS is second with 67 and ABC, which will televise the Emmys, is fourth with 55.
Such a strong showing by a relatively new programmer like HBO is an indication of how fragmented television has become and how cable is continuing to chip away at the networks' dominance.
"HBO views this as a real acknowledgment of the good work we've done," said a company spokeswoman. "We're up there with the best of them, and it really feels nice."
HBO also came out far ahead of Fox, the unofficial fourth network, which was nominated 17 times.

Unlike network programs, which reach virtually every household that has a TV set, HBO has a comparatively small 23 million subscribers. Despite this much narrower penetration and the fact that cable has only been eligible for Emmys since 1988, HBO has consistently made a strong showing at the awards show. In 1993 it walked away with 59 awards, more than any of the networks.

A common rebuttal that HBO's success comes from its focus on cinema-quality films and miniseries of a different sort than the networks produce is also beginning to ring hollow. This year, HBO got most of its nominations for its sitcom "The Larry Sanders Show," a series about a fictional talk show host, that was behind only "E.R" and "Chicago Hope" in terms of total nominations.
Other cable stations receiving multiple Emmy nominations include Turner Network Television (TNT) with 16 and The Disney Channel, which is up for seven awards.
Because Emmys are based on the votes of a relatively small group of industry peers rather than broad audiences, they are seen as a measure of quality rather than popularity.
In recent years, however, the two have gone hand in hand, marking a change from past decades when hits like "Happy Days" and "Three's Company" were often snubbed at the Emmys.
Some industry officials say much of the credit for improving the overall quality of popular television also goes to cable stations.
"We have never seen shows as spectacular as the things being offered now," said Murray Weissman, spokesman for the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences.
"I think it's because the competition has gotten so stiff. There must be 30 cable networks spinning out shows and some are doing very aggressive work."
Other popular shows poised to win big at this year's awards are ABC's police drama "NYPD Blue," NBC's "Seinfeld" and Fox's "The X-Files."

But the awards show will not be entirely without suspense, especially for Angela Lansbury, nominated for best actress in a drama series. The longtime star of CBS' "Murder She Wrote," which just concluded its final season, has been nominated for 16 Emmys over her career, but has never won.
